blocks.text: AN OPEN COLLECTION THESE RECORDS CAME FROM

Wikidata holds no object. It is how the named objects were resolved: each one was looked up once, checked against its expected name, and rejected if it turned out to be a person or a modern paper. The photographs come from Wikimedia Commons, each with its own licence and its own photographer.
What we hold for this collection.
Wikimedia Commons · no author recorded by the source (opens in a new tab) Public domain
Fourteenth-century BC diplomatic archive naming Canaanite city-states.
archive, written on clay tablets, primarily consisting of diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian administration and its representatives in Canaan and Amurru during the New Kingdom
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-058 Late Bronze Age political and geographic context
What it supports. Berlin's museum catalog identifies EA289 as correspondence from Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem within the Amarna archive.
What it does not. Habiru terminology cannot simply be equated with biblical Hebrews; these letters do not independently narrate Joshua's conquest.
Bears on: Canaan and Jerusalem before Israel's monarchy

פעמי-עליון (opens in a new tab) CC BY-SA 4.0 · share-alike
Hebrew ostraca from the Judahite fort at Arad.
collection of more than 100 inscribed pottery shards
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-044 administrative and writing context
What it supports. Arad military correspondence documents late-monarchic Judahite administration; the authors discuss a reference to the house of YHWH.
What it does not. A literacy analysis cannot directly date the composition of individual biblical books or prove their narratives.
Bears on: Judah's military and religious administration

human whose existence is disputed; mythical character
SpeakingArch (opens in a new tab) CC BY-SA 4.0 · share-alike
Old Babylonian flood and creation poem.
human whose existence is disputed; mythical character
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-117 flood literary parallels; global-event claim unestablished
What it supports. The museum catalogs an Atrahasis flood-text fragment; its object trail separately describes Gilgamesh's eleventh tablet and Utnapishtim.
What it does not. Literary flood traditions and local flood deposits do not establish a single simultaneous global flood. Regional sediment sequences were not individually audited.

Jastrow (opens in a new tab) Public domain
Ugaritic stele of Baal, the deity the prophets contend with.
Department of Near Eastern Antiquities of the Louvre
Its reach, and its limit. Iconography supplies visual context for the Baal cult. It provides no archaeological verification of Elijah's miracle.

Shows Jehu of Israel, or his envoy, bringing tribute to Shalmaneser III.
black limestone Assyrian sculpture with inscriptions
Its reach, and its limit. Names Jehu's tribute; depicted kneeling figure may be a representative.

Mediatus/Kopie eines Originalbriefes; Kopist unbekannt (opens in a new tab) Public domain
Early Greek biblical papyri including P66 and P75.
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-096 Gospel textual transmission
What it supports. The Vatican Library publishes transcription and images of Luke11 and John1 in Bodmer XIV-XV, P75; Bodmer's foundation separately identifies P66 as John.
What it does not. The sampled pages verify textual witnesses, not every Bodmer papyrus or the historicity of the Gospel events; paleographic dates are estimates.
Bears on: Luke, John and other biblical books

Shoshenq I's campaign list, beside the Shishak invasion of 1 Kings 14.
No Wikidata item exists for this object. Recorded from its Wikimedia Commons category of photographs.
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-011 historical campaign context
What it supports. The Bubastite Portal preserves Shoshenq I's royal imagery and a southern-Levant place list.
What it does not. The Shishak identification is historical comparison; preserved names do not independently document the plundering of Jerusalem.

Its reach, and its limit. Widely identified with the high priest's family; bones are not independently identified individuals.

Old Babylonian law stele, the standard comparison for the Mosaic law codes.
Babylonian code of law or conduct
Its reach, and its limit. Provides a primary comparative source for ancient Near Eastern law. Legal parallels neither establish direct copying nor prove divine origin.

Israel Museum (opens in a new tab) Public domain
15,000 fragments of about 850 scrolls from ancient Judaism
archaeological artefact; group of manuscripts; discovered text
ARCHAEOLOGY CATALOGUE · ROW BA-088 biblical textual transmission
What it supports. IAA's catalog identifies biblical scrolls from Qumran and displays dated, named examples.
What it does not. The corpus contains textual variants and non-biblical works; preservation of a biblical text is not independent verification of its narrated events.
